strengths: The paper studies a useful question: whether demonstrations on procedurally generated primitive compositions can support grasping of unseen everyday objects. The physical toy dataset and experiments on two robot embodiments represent substantial engineering effort.
The reported transfer results are promising: 80% success on simulated YCB objects, 66.67% on real Franka YCB objects, and 50.77% on the humanoid’s 13-object evaluation.
Detection pooling produces a substantial improvement within the same policy architecture in simulation: 80% versus 51.63% for attention pooling and 40.58% for mean pooling at 2,500 demonstrations.
The paper investigates demonstration count, object diversity, policy size, primitive types, complexity, and color, and provides useful hardware, manufacturing, and training details.
weaknesses: The headline superiority claim conflicts with the main real-world results. Table 2 reports 76.56% for π0-FAST finetuned on the same toy demonstrations, versus 66.67% for LEGO. Although Section 5.3 acknowledges this, the abstract, introduction, and conclusion broadly claim to outperform the state of the art. The evidence supports competitive transfer with a smaller policy, not the stated overall superiority.

Pretraining and model-size comparisons are misleading. LEGO uses a pretrained MVP ViT-L encoder, SAM 2, and a separately trained Faster R-CNN detector, yet Table 2 marks it as having no pretraining and the text repeatedly describes training from scratch. The quoted 86M parameters describe the policy transformer rather than the complete system. Full-system parameter counts, pretraining dependencies, and inference costs are needed to substantiate efficiency claims.

The central mechanism is insufficiently isolated. Detection pooling supplies explicit target segmentation, whereas the pooling baselines do not receive equivalent object information. There are no comparisons against object crops, background masking, mask-conditioned policies, or separate ablations of attention masking and final masked pooling. Moreover, all pooling ablations use ground-truth simulation masks; no real-world ablation establishes that DetPool causes the reported physical-robot gains.

The experiments demonstrate that toy training can work, but do not establish the distinctive value of the proposed toy distribution. Missing controls include matched demonstration budgets on ordinary objects and alternative procedural shapes. Related object-centric methods, particularly OTTER, are discussed but not evaluated, and standard imitation-learning baselines such as ACT or Diffusion Policy are absent. Consequently, the contribution beyond combining synthetic objects, segmentation, and behavior cloning remains unclear.

Baseline behavior requires stronger validation. In simulation, OpenVLA-OFT falls from 36.35% to 12.79% as demonstrations increase, while π0-FAST remains near failure. The proposed explanations of overfitting and data hunger are not supported by training diagnostics or systematic tuning. Camera inputs, action representations, and checkpoint selection also differ across methods. Appendix H even uses different simulated success thresholds, favoring OpenVLA-OFT; although this does not explain LEGO’s advantage, it prevents a uniform comparison.

Uncertainty and reproducibility are incomplete. Results lack repeated training seeds and confidence intervals, and the humanoid evaluation contains only five trials per object with acknowledged hand hardware problems. Detector accuracy on unseen objects, segmentation failure handling, encoder freezing, and end-to-end control latency are not adequately characterized. The controlled placement evaluations support a narrower conclusion than robust general-purpose grasping.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: learning grasping policies that transfer to unseen objects with limited robot demonstrations. Procedurally generated, printable toys provide a practical and reproducible training-object design.

The experimental effort is substantial, spanning simulation, a physical Franka robot, and a humanoid hand. Reported success rates of 80% in simulation, 66.67% on real YCB objects, and 50.77% on the humanoid demonstrate useful transfer.

The simulation pooling comparison provides concrete positive evidence: DetPool achieves 80% versus 51.63% for attention pooling with 2,500 demonstrations. Studies of dataset size, model size, primitive types, and color provide additional empirical coverage.
weaknesses: The central architectural contribution is insufficiently isolated. DetPool combines externally supplied segmentation, restricted self-attention, and masked pooling, whereas the pooling baselines lack equivalent object supervision. Comparisons against masked-image inputs, object crops, masked pooling without attention restriction, and attention restriction without masked pooling are needed. No real-world DetPool ablation establishes that it causes the headline physical-robot improvement.

The distinctive benefit of compositional toys remains unproven. There is no matched-budget comparison against training on ordinary objects, alternative procedural shapes, or a diverse collection of individual primitives. Table 5 compares only compositions of two through five primitives. Consequently, the results establish that toy training can transfer, but not that the proposed construction is especially effective or that compositional structure explains generalization.

The baseline suite does not adequately establish competitiveness for grasping. It emphasizes large VLAs and ShapeGrasp, omitting strong specialist grasping systems and compact imitation-learning baselines such as ACT or diffusion policies. OTTER, identified as the closest representation approach, is not evaluated. The severe deterioration of both VLA baselines with increasing simulation data requires stronger diagnosis than speculative explanations about overfitting.

The pretraining and efficiency comparisons are misleading. Table 2 marks LEGO as having no pretraining, and the text repeatedly describes training from scratch, despite using pretrained MVP ViT-L features and a perception pipeline containing Faster R-CNN and SAM 2. The quoted 86M parameters count the policy transformer rather than the complete system. Full-system parameter counts, inference latency, and a clear distinction between policy training and pretrained perception are necessary.

The headline superiority claim overstates the real-world evidence. Fine-tuned π0-FAST reaches 76.56% on Franka, exceeding LEGO's 66.67% by 9.89 percentage points with the same toy fine-tuning dataset. Section 5.3 acknowledges this, but the abstract and conclusion broadly claim superiority over state-of-the-art approaches. Lower task-specific data requirements are promising, but do not establish an overall performance advantage.

Evaluation uncertainty and protocol inconsistencies weaken confidence. No repeated-training variability or confidence intervals are reported, and humanoid evaluation comprises only five trials per object. Appendix H applies different simulation success thresholds to OpenVLA-OFT and other methods, preventing a uniform comparison even though this favors the baseline. Additionally, 66.67% cannot arise from the stated 64 × 16 equally weighted binary Franka trials; the actual denominator or aggregation procedure needs clarification.

The generalization and scaling claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Testing primarily concerns object changes within fixed robot and camera setups; scene, clutter, occlusion, and segmentation robustness are not systematically evaluated. Simulation uses ground-truth masks. Figure 4 also does not show consistently improving performance with greater toy diversity, and the absence of repeated dataset sampling makes the claimed relative importance of demonstration count and diversity uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: learning grasping policies that transfer to unseen objects from a modest demonstration dataset. Procedurally generated, physically printable toys offer a useful and reproducible experimental approach.
The simulation results provide substantial evidence that object-focused representations help: DetPool achieves 80.00% success versus 51.63% for attention pooling with 2,500 demonstrations.
Physical experiments represent substantial effort and extend beyond one embodiment: the method reports 66.67% success on 64 YCB objects with Franka and 50.77% on 13 objects with a humanoid hand.
The studies of demonstration count, object diversity, primitive types, and policy size provide useful empirical observations.
weaknesses: The headline superiority claim is overstated. Table 2 reports 76.56% for π0-FAST fine-tuned on the same toy demonstrations, versus 66.67% for LEGO. Although the experimental discussion acknowledges this, the abstract and conclusion claim superiority over state-of-the-art approaches without this qualification.

The central DetPool claim is insufficiently isolated. Its comparisons against standard pooling change both access to explicit object segmentation and the pooling mechanism. Missing controls include object crops, masked images, and object-token pooling without internal attention masking. Furthermore, no real-world DetPool ablation establishes that this mechanism explains the physical-robot results.

Pretraining and model-size comparisons are misleading. The method uses a pretrained MVP ViT-L encoder, SAM 2, and a separately trained detector, yet Table 2 marks pretraining as absent and the text describes training from scratch. The reported 86M parameters describe the policy transformer rather than the complete system. These distinctions materially affect the claimed data and computational advantages.

The evaluation does not adequately establish competitiveness against targeted alternatives. Strong grasp-specific systems and compact imitation-learning baselines with comparable visual inputs are missing. VLA comparisons use different camera inputs, action parameterizations, and training schedules; the severe deterioration of OpenVLA-OFT as data increases is attributed to overfitting without supporting diagnostics.

The contribution of the toy construction itself remains unclear. There is no demonstration-budget-matched comparison against ordinary training objects or alternative procedural shape distributions. Consequently, the experiments demonstrate that these toys can support transfer, but do not establish that their particular compositional design provides an advantage.

Uncertainty and deployment robustness are underexplored. Results lack repeated training seeds or confidence intervals, and the humanoid evaluation contains only 65 trials with acknowledged hardware problems. Simulation uses ground-truth masks, while real deployment relies on a detector and SAM 2 without segmentation-error or latency analysis. These limitations leave the broader robustness and scaling claims insufficiently supported.

strengths: The procedural toy dataset offers a practical, interpretable approach to studying object generalization. Collecting demonstrations with 250 physical toys and evaluating two robot embodiments represents substantial experimental effort.

The reported transfer results are promising: 80% simulated YCB grasping success, 66.67% real Franka success, and 50.77% humanoid success. The Franka evaluation covers 64 objects with 16 placements each.
The controlled pooling comparison provides meaningful evidence for object-focused representations: DetPool reaches 80% versus 51.63% for attention pooling at 2,500 demonstrations.

The appendix substantially strengthens the evaluation through additional object-centric baselines, lighting and clutter tests, bounding-box perturbations, control and temporal-context ablations, and a pushing task. Hardware, training, and manufacturing details are also provided.
weaknesses: The central attribution to DetPool is insufficiently isolated. DetPool receives target segmentation information unavailable to the standard pooling baselines. Comparisons against masked images, object crops, and object-token pooling without internal attention masking are needed to distinguish the proposed mechanism from simply supplying object localization. No real-world DetPool ablation establishes that it explains the physical-robot gains.

Baseline comparisons contain consequential confounds. OpenVLA-OFT uses delta joint control while LEGO uses absolute control; Table 16 shows this choice alone changes LEGO's success from 37.02% to 80%. Camera inputs and checkpoint-selection procedures also differ. The unusually poor simulation results and deterioration with additional data require stronger diagnostic evidence before supporting broad superiority claims.

The pretraining and model-size presentation is misleading. LEGO uses a pretrained MVP ViT-L, SAM 2, and an additional detector trained on 200 annotated images, yet Table 2 marks pretraining as absent and the text describes training from scratch. The quoted 86M parameters cover the policy transformer rather than the complete perception-and-control pipeline. Claims about data and computational efficiency should account for these components.

The abstract and conclusion overstate comparative performance. On the principal real Franka benchmark, fine-tuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56%, exceeding LEGO's 66.67% by approximately 10 percentage points. LEGO's performance with limited task demonstrations remains interesting, but the strongest matched toy-finetuning baseline wins.

The necessity and distinctiveness of the toy construction are not established. There is no matched-budget comparison against ordinary training objects or alternative procedural geometry distributions. Primitive-removal and complexity ablations characterize the chosen dataset but do not establish that its compositional design is responsible for efficient transfer. Likewise, novel object identities and Chamfer-distance buckets alone do not establish the claimed strong out-of-distribution separation.

Statistical support and reproducibility remain incomplete. Main comparisons and scaling curves lack variability across training seeds or sampled toy sets; the humanoid evaluation has only five trials per object and reported hardware problems. Appendix F describes final-feature masking without clearly documenting the internal attention blocking central to Section 3.3. Encoder freezing, end-to-end inference cost, and validation protocols also need clarification.

strengths: The procedural toy dataset provides a concrete, reproducible approach to studying generalization across object shapes, supported by substantial simulation and physical data collection.
The transfer results are promising: 80% success on simulated YCB objects, 66.67% on real Franka grasping, and 50.77% across 13 objects with a humanoid hand.
Table 1 provides strong evidence that the complete DetPool mechanism helps within the proposed architecture: at 2,500 demonstrations, it achieves 80% versus 51.63% for attention pooling.
The appendix adds useful experiments on object-centric baselines, lighting, clutter, mask perturbations, pushing, temporal context, and action parameterization.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons have substantial confounds. OpenVLA-OFT uses delta joint control, whereas LEGO uses absolute control; Table 16 shows that this choice alone changes LEGO's success from 37.02% to 80%. Camera inputs and checkpoint selection also differ. The unusually poor baseline results and degradation with additional data require controlled diagnosis before supporting broad superiority claims.

Pretraining and model-size claims are misleading. LEGO uses a pretrained MVP ViT-L encoder, SAM 2, and a separately trained Faster R-CNN detector, yet Table 2 marks pretraining as absent and the text repeatedly describes training from scratch. The reported 86M parameters describe the policy transformer rather than the complete system. Consequently, the claimed pretraining independence and efficiency advantages are not established by the reported accounting.

The headline comparison overstates the results. On the main real-world Franka benchmark, fine-tuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56%, exceeding LEGO's 66.67%. Although the results section acknowledges this, the abstract and conclusion broadly claim superiority over state-of-the-art models, including π0-FAST.

The central methodological claim is insufficiently isolated. DetPool combines target segmentation, restricted attention, and masked pooling, but the ablations do not separately test these components or compare against straightforward masked-image or object-crop alternatives using equivalent supervision. There is also no physical-robot DetPool ablation. Thus, the evidence establishes the benefit of the combined pipeline more clearly than the novelty or necessity of the proposed attention mechanism.

The distinctive value of compositional toys remains uncertain. There is no matched-budget comparison against training on ordinary objects, alternative procedural shapes, or a complete primitives-only dataset. The scaling and complexity studies are informative, but do not establish that this particular toy construction is especially effective. Random construction also does not itself establish strong distributional separation from everyday object geometry.

Evaluation uncertainty limits several conclusions. Main comparisons and scaling curves lack repeated training seeds and uncertainty estimates; humanoid evaluation uses only five trials per object and reports hardware problems. Simulation clutter experiments use ground-truth target masks, so they do not establish autonomous target discrimination. The additional object-centric baselines lack enough implementation detail to interpret results such as GROOT's 1.54% success confidently.

strengths: The paper explores a useful, concrete question: whether demonstrations on procedurally composed primitive objects can support grasping of unseen everyday objects. The physical toy dataset and experiments on two robot embodiments represent substantial effort.
DetPool produces large improvements over standard pooling within the same policy architecture: 80.00% versus 51.63% for attention pooling with 2,500 simulation demonstrations.
Physical evaluations provide encouraging evidence of object generalization, with reported success rates of 66.67% on Franka and 50.77% on the humanoid hand.

The appendix substantially broadens the evaluation through additional object-centric baselines, lighting and clutter tests, mask perturbations, a pushing task, and architectural ablations. Hardware, training, and manufacturing details are also provided.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is insufficiently isolated. Standard pooling baselines do not receive equivalent object-mask information, so their comparison conflates object localization with the proposed attention restriction. Masked final pooling, object cropping, and attention-masking-only controls are needed, alongside a physical-robot DetPool ablation. Appendix F also describes masking final features without clearly documenting the within-transformer attention restriction specified in Section 3.3.

Baseline comparisons contain consequential confounds. OpenVLA-OFT uses delta joint control, whereas LEGO uses absolute control; Table 16 shows that this choice alone changes LEGO's simulation performance from 37.02% to 80.00%. Camera inputs and checkpoint-selection procedures also differ. The extremely low baseline results and OpenVLA's deterioration with additional data need stronger diagnostics before supporting broad superiority claims.

The headline comparison overstates the real-world findings. Fine-tuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56%, exceeding LEGO's 66.67% under the same toy-demonstration budget. LEGO's advantage over the untuned model is encouraging but does not establish superiority over the strongest adapted baseline.

Pretraining and model-size accounting are misleading. LEGO uses a pretrained MVP ViT-L and SAM 2, plus a separately trained detector, yet Table 2 marks pretraining as absent and the text repeatedly describes training from scratch. The advertised 86M parameters describe the policy transformer rather than the complete perception-and-control system. These distinctions materially affect the claimed data and computational efficiency.

The specific value of primitive composition remains under-established. There is no matched comparison against training on ordinary objects, alternative procedural shapes, or an appropriately controlled primitive-only dataset. Existing object-centric methods are discussed and some are evaluated, but the closest cited approach, OTTER, is not compared experimentally. The conceptual novelty of masking and pooling therefore needs stronger positioning and controlled evidence.

Statistical support and protocol consistency need improvement. Main results and scaling curves lack repeated-training uncertainty; the humanoid evaluation has only five trials per object. The reported 66.67% Franka result also requires reconciliation with the stated 64 objects × 16 binary trials. Simulation robustness largely assumes ground-truth target masks, and bounding-box perturbations do not establish robustness to real detector failures. These limitations weaken the broader generalization and scaling claims.
